title: P-VALUES
body:
$$
p = P(\text{a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one} \mid H_0 \text{ is true})
$$

**Everything in that line matters, especially the conditioning bar.** A $p$-value assumes the null
is true and asks how surprising your data would be in that world. Small $p$ means the data sits
awkwardly with $H_0$, so $H_0$ is what gets rejected. See [[Hypothesis Testing]] for where it sits
in the procedure.

"At least as extreme" is what makes it a tail area rather than a point probability, and it is
computed from the [[Probability Density Function|CDF]] of the null distribution: normal, $t$,
$\chi^2$, or $F$ depending on the test. Two-tailed tests double the one-tail area, which is why the
same data gives a $p$ twice as large under a two-sided alternative.

## The decision

$p < \alpha$ rejects. That is the whole rule, and the comparison is against an $\alpha$ chosen
**before** seeing the data. $\alpha = 0.05$ is convention and nothing more; there is no property of
the universe that changes at $0.05$, and treating $p = 0.049$ and $p = 0.051$ as different findings
is the clearest symptom of taking the threshold too seriously.

## The three things it is not

> [!warning] Misreadings, in order of how often they happen
> 1. **Not $P(H_0 \text{ is true})$.** It is $P(\text{data} \mid H_0)$, and those two conditionals
>    are related by [[Bayes Theorem]], which needs a prior the frequentist framework does not have.
>    The medical-test example in that note is the same trap: $P(+ \mid D)$ was 0.99 and
>    $P(D \mid +)$ was 0.02.
> 2. **Not the probability you are wrong.** The probability of a false rejection is $\alpha$, fixed
>    in advance, and it is a property of the procedure across all its uses rather than of this
>    result. See [[Type I and Type II Errors]].
> 3. **Not a measure of effect size or importance.** $p$ depends on $n$ as much as on the effect,
>    so a trivial difference reaches $p < 0.001$ given enough data and a large one misses
>    significance in a small study. A [[Confidence Interval]] shows the size; the $p$-value shows
>    only whether zero is plausible.

A fourth, which is really the first restated: a large $p$ is **not** evidence that $H_0$ is true. It
is evidence that your data did not distinguish it from the alternative, which is also what a
badly underpowered study produces.

## $p$-hacking

The $p$-value's guarantee holds for **one pre-specified test**. Run twenty independent tests at
$\alpha = 0.05$ on pure noise and one comes back significant on average, because that is exactly
what a 5% false positive rate means. So the practices that break it are all versions of testing
more than once and reporting the winner:

- trying many outcome variables and publishing the one that worked
- collecting more data until $p$ dips below the line, then stopping
- deciding on a one-tailed alternative after seeing which way the difference ran
- splitting the sample into subgroups and testing each

[[ANOVA]] exists precisely to avoid the first version of this when comparing several group means,
by asking one question instead of $\binom{k}{2}$.
